unit.title: Apply knowledge of Team Jamaica requirements in the workplace

summary: This unit prepares you to work with visitors the Team Jamaica way: with courtesy and a warm welcome, harassment-free service, sound safety advice, and knowledge of Jamaica's history, culture and environment. You will learn what to do when a visitor is bothered, hurt or in trouble, and how to use these standards in your daily work in a villa, hotel or kitchen.

blocks.p: Tourism is one of Jamaica's biggest earners and employers. Visitors judge the island by the people they meet: the person at the gate, the cook, the driver, the housekeeper. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. It teaches the standards of **Team Jamaica** and how to apply them at work.
You do not need to be a guide or a historian to use this unit. You need to be **courteous, honest, safe and well informed**, and to know how to help a visitor who is worried, bothered or in trouble.

What this means at work

Who runs it, who it is for, and why it matters
Check the rules for the certificate with the agency

Be patient, honest and helpful
Give harassment-free service

Help a visitor who is being bothered, safely and calmly
Give sound safety and security advice
Sea, sun, valuables, transport
Emergency numbers and what to do in an emergency

Lost passport, theft, illness, hurricane warning, complaint
Share knowledge of Jamaica
National symbols, heroes, history, parishes, food, music, places
Give facts correctly, and say 'I will find out' when unsure
Care for the environment
Do not litter; save water and power; protect coral and wildlife
Keep professional standards
Neat appearance, punctual, honest, respectful, no pressure to buy

Welcome the visitor

Deal with problems

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre: a role play of a warm welcome and harassment-free care, and a 'Know Jamaica' display with a pocket safety card. The assessor watches your manner, your accuracy and your safety advice.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph the display and your group at work. Do not photograph a person's face unless they agree and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Team Jamaica** is a training programme run by **TPDCo**, the **Tourism Product Development Company**, for people who work with visitors. TPDCo is the agency of Jamaica's tourism ministry that works to improve the island's tourism product: its attractions, standards and the people who serve visitors.

ul: People who work with visitors: hotel and villa staff, tour guides, drivers, craft vendors, attraction staff, watersports operators and many others.
Villa staff are in a special position: they live and work close to guests, and guests ask them for advice every day.
How long the certificate lasts, how it is renewed and what the course covers are set by TPDCo. Check the **current** rules with TPDCo or your instructor, because they can change.

head: Topic
Why it matters
rows: Courtesy and customer service
Visitors who feel welcome enjoy their stay and return.
The warm Jamaican welcome
It is part of what makes Jamaica different.
Visitor safety and security
A safe visitor is a happy visitor.
Harassment-free service
Visitors who feel pressured leave with a bad memory and tell others.
Product knowledge: history, culture, attractions
Visitors ask questions and trust knowledgeable staff.
Caring for the environment
Beaches, reefs and rivers are what visitors come to see.

blocks.p: A tourism worker is sometimes called an **ambassador** for Jamaica, because a visitor often knows only a few Jamaicans. How you behave shapes how that visitor sees the whole country. A warm greeting, an honest answer or a small act of kindness can be told and re-told, and one rude moment can be too.

ul: Visitors tell family and friends, and post reviews online. Good reviews bring more visitors.
More visitors mean more jobs, more income for families and more business for local farmers, drivers, craft makers and cooks.
Harassment or poor service does the opposite: fewer visitors, fewer jobs.

blocks.note: The Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) markets Jamaica to the world. TPDCo works on standards and product quality at home. Both rely on every worker doing a good job.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Smile and make eye contact
Greet: 'Good morning' or 'Welcome to Jamaica'
Use the guest's name and title
Introduce yourself
Offer help, such as bags or a cool drink
Listen to what the guest needs
Follow up and thank them

ul: Greet every guest warmly, with a smile, a clear greeting and good eye contact.
Use the guest's name and title (Mr, Mrs, Dr) until they ask you to use their first name.
Offer help **before** you are asked: carry bags, bring a cool drink, point out the way to the beach.
Remember small details, such as a favourite drink or fruit. They make the welcome personal.
Thank guests and wish them well when they leave.
Speak **slowly and clearly, in simple English**, if a guest has trouble with your accent. Do not shout, and do not use only Patois with a guest who does not understand it.
Look at the guest and listen to the whole question before you answer.
Be **patient**. A visitor may be tired from travel, new to the island, or unsure about the local customs. They may ask the same question that other guests asked an hour ago.
Repeat important instructions, and write them down if needed: directions, times, phone numbers.
If you do not know the answer, say: 'I will find out for you.' Then find out and tell them.
Give **correct** information: prices, opening times, distances, safety advice.
Do not make up an answer. A wrong answer can send a guest to a closed attraction or into danger.
Recommend places and services that suit the guest, not only the ones that pay you.

blocks.p: If a visitor asks for directions, give clear, simple directions with landmarks, or write them down. If you are unsure, check with a colleague, a map or a phone. Suggest a licensed taxi or tour if the place is far.

ul: Stay calm and polite. Do not argue.
Listen, say you understand, and say what you can do.
If you cannot solve the problem, pass it to your supervisor and tell the guest who will help.
Never speak badly of a guest, or of another worker, in front of guests.

blocks.p: Treat every guest equally, whatever their country, colour, religion, age, disability or background. Respect their privacy and property. Do not enter a guest's room without good reason and permission, do not touch their belongings and do not ask personal questions.

blocks.note: 'Out of Many, One People' is Jamaica's motto. In tourism it means that every guest, and every worker, is part of one welcoming community.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Visitor harassment** is any behaviour that annoys, pressures, frightens or embarrasses a visitor against their wishes. It often happens when someone will not accept a visitor's 'no, thank you'.

head: Examples of harassment
Why it is wrong
rows: Following a visitor and blocking the way until they buy
It frightens the visitor and takes away their choice.
Offering drugs again and again
It is illegal as well as unwelcome.
Touching a visitor's hair to braid it, or touching them, without being asked
It invades their personal space.
Grabbing bags at a gate to carry them for money
It puts the visitor under pressure.
Shouting rude or sexual remarks
It is offensive and can be unlawful.
Ignoring 'no' and continuing to push
It shows no respect.

ul: Visitors feel unsafe and uncomfortable.
They stay inside their hotel or villa and spend less money in local communities.
They tell family and friends, and post bad reviews online.
Fewer people choose to visit, so fewer jobs and less income for Jamaicans.
It harms the good name of the whole island, including honest workers.
**Offer a service once**, explain it clearly, and **accept the answer**. 'No, thank you' means no.
Never pressure a guest to buy, tip or book anything.
Never touch a guest without permission.
Do not follow guests along the beach or road.
Advise guests before they go out: use licensed tours and transport, keep valuables out of sight, and say a polite but clear 'no, thank you' and keep walking.
Report people who regularly bother visitors near the villa to your supervisor or the police.

blocks.h: How you help a visitor who is being harassed

flow: Stay calm and polite; do not shout or fight
Step in safely and move close to the visitor
Say something like: 'Excuse me, the guest is with me'
Help the visitor move away, politely but firmly
If the person will not stop, or there is a threat or drugs, call security or the police on **119**
Check that the visitor is all right
Write down what happened and tell your supervisor

head: Situation
Best response
rows: A vendor keeps pushing a guest after the guest says no
Politely help the guest move on; report it if it continues.
A man on the beach keeps offering a guest drugs
Reassure the guest; report it to security or the police.
A guest wants a tour
Offer it once, explain it, and accept the answer.
A colleague is rude to a visitor
Help the visitor first; then speak to the supervisor.
A visitor is about to buy a tour from a stranger
Suggest booking with a licensed operator.

blocks.note: Do not argue or fight with a person who is harassing a visitor. Your job is to protect the visitor calmly, not to win. If you feel unsafe, call for help.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Many Jamaicans earn an honest living from vendors' stalls, craft markets and tours. Harassment-free service does not mean ignoring them: it means courtesy in both directions. Visitors are free to say no, and vendors should accept that.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Number
Service
rows: Police
Fire brigade and ambulance
The villa's own number
Keep it on the guest's pocket card and by the phone

blocks.p: Know the numbers by heart, and know the nearest hospital, police station and the way to your villa's address.

head: Risk
Advice to give
rows: Sea and beach
Swim only where it is safe and, where flags are used, **never swim when a red flag is flying**
Do not swim alone, at night, or after drinking alcohol
Watch children at all times near the sea and the villa pool; keep the pool gate closed
Sun and heat
Use sunscreen, wear a hat and drink plenty of water
Stay in the shade in the middle of the day
Valuables
Keep passports, cash and valuables in the villa safe
Carry only what is needed
Lock doors and windows when going out or at night
Transport and tours
Use **licensed, approved** tour and taxi operators
Book through the villa or a licensed operator, not a stranger on the street
Walking alone, especially at night
Advise against walking alone on a quiet beach or road late at night, and suggest a safer plan, such as a taxi or a group.
Drugs and strangers
Say a polite 'no, thank you' and keep walking; report persistent offers.

head: Problem
What you do
rows: A guest is hurt or ill
Keep calm, give first aid you are trained to give, call 110 for an ambulance if needed, and tell your supervisor.
A guest feels faint after a long time in the sun
Move them to shade, give water, loosen tight clothing, and get help if they do not recover quickly.
A guest loses their passport
Help them report it to the police, then contact their embassy or consulate.
A guest's bag is stolen
Make sure they are safe, help them report it to the police (119), and help them block bank cards. Write an incident report.
A guest is in a car or boat accident
Call 110 and the police (119); stay with them; tell your supervisor.

blocks.p: Jamaica's hurricane season runs from June to November. Follow the villa's **hurricane plan** and information from the Meteorological Service and the **ODPEM** (Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management). Keep guests informed and safe.

ul: Check the plan: shutters, loose items, water, torches, batteries, a first aid kit, food and the phone numbers of guests' embassies.
Tell guests clearly and calmly what is happening and what to do. Do not frighten them.
Do not send guests out to travel in dangerous weather. Follow the instructions of the authorities.
Check on every guest afterwards and report damage to your supervisor.
Write what happened, when, where and who was involved.
Write what you did, and who you told.
Use facts, not opinions. Give it to your supervisor the same day.

blocks.note: Never promise a guest more than you can do. If you say 'I will call the police for you', do it, and tell the guest what happens next.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Guests ask staff about Jamaica all the time. You do not need to know everything, but the facts you give must be correct. Learn the basics below, and say 'I will find out' when you are not sure.

head: Symbol
What it is
rows: Flag
Black, green and gold, with a gold diagonal cross: black for the strength and creativity of the people, gold for the natural wealth and beauty of sunlight, green for hope and agricultural resources.
Motto
'Out of Many, One People'.
National bird
The doctor bird, a hummingbird with long tail feathers.
National flower
Lignum vitae, with small blue flowers.
National tree
The blue mahoe.
National fruit
The ackee.
National dish
Ackee and saltfish.

blocks.p: Jamaica has **seven National Heroes**. National Heroes' Day is observed on the **third Monday in October**.

head: Hero
Known for
rows: Nanny of the Maroons
Maroon leader who resisted slavery; the only woman among the heroes.
Sam Sharpe
Led the 1831 Christmas Rebellion (the Baptist War), which helped bring slavery to an end.
Paul Bogle
Led the 1865 Morant Bay Rebellion.
George William Gordon
Politician and landowner linked to the Morant Bay events; executed in 1865.
Marcus Garvey
Founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA); spoke for black pride and self-reliance.
Sir Alexander Bustamante
Labour leader and first Prime Minister of independent Jamaica.
Norman Manley
Lawyer and politician; founded the People's National Party; Premier before independence.

head: When
What happened
rows: Before 1494
The **Taíno** lived on the island; they called it **Xaymaca**, usually said to mean 'land of wood and water'.
Christopher Columbus reached Jamaica for Spain.
1509 onwards
Spanish settlement; the Taíno people declined.
The English (British) took the island from Spain.
An earthquake destroyed much of Port Royal.
Sugar estates grew and many Africans were brought in slavery. **Maroons**, Africans who escaped slavery and lived free in the hills, kept their freedom; treaties were made with them in 1739.
Sam Sharpe's Christmas Rebellion.
Slavery was abolished in 1834 (Emancipation, 1 August), with full freedom from the apprenticeship system on 1 August 1838. 1 August is a public holiday, Emancipation Day.
Morant Bay Rebellion.
Independence: **6 August 1962**.

ul: Jamaica is an island in the **Caribbean Sea**, south of Cuba. It has **14 parishes** in three counties: Cornwall, Middlesex and Surrey. The capital is **Kingston**.
The official language is English. Many Jamaicans also speak **Patois** (Patwa), a language that mixes English with West African and other words.
The currency is the Jamaican dollar (J$). The electricity supply is 110 V at 50 Hz.
The Blue Mountains rise to over 2,200 m. Jamaican **Blue Mountain coffee** is famous around the world.

head: Topic
What you can tell a guest
rows: Music
Jamaica created mento, ska, rocksteady, reggae and dancehall. Reggae was made famous worldwide by Bob Marley. Visit the Bob Marley Museum in Kingston, or his birthplace at Nine Mile, St Ann.
Food
Jerk chicken and pork (**Boston Bay** in Portland is well known for jerk), ackee and saltfish, curry goat, bammy, festival, patties, and sorrel at Christmas. Try fruit in season.
Places
Dunn's River Falls (Ocho Rios), Negril's long beach and cliffs, Martha Brae rafting (Trelawny), Port Antonio and the Blue Lagoon, the Blue Mountains, Port Royal, YS Falls (St Elizabeth).
Festivals and days
Emancipation Day (1 August), Independence Day (6 August), National Heroes' Day (third Monday in October).

ul: A guest who asks about the Maroons: they were Africans who escaped slavery and lived free in the hills. Their towns include Accompong in St Elizabeth, and Moore Town in Portland.
Share your pride in Jamaica in a friendly way: point out a doctor bird in the garden, serve ackee and saltfish at breakfast and explain it, or tell a hero's story when you pass a monument.
Keep your facts correct and answer questions honestly.

blocks.note: A display or a pocket card for guests must have **correct facts**. Check each fact in a reliable source and write the source down, as your practical requires.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Many visitors come to Jamaica for its beaches, coral reefs, rivers, waterfalls, mountains and wildlife. If these are damaged, the island becomes less attractive, fewer visitors come and jobs are lost.

ul: **Coral reefs** are alive. They protect the coast from storms and are home to fish. Once broken, they take many years to recover.
Litter spoils beaches, harms sea life and spreads disease.
Water and power are limited resources that cost money. Saving them helps the villa and the country.
A clean island is healthier and nicer to live in and to visit.
**Never litter**, and pick up litter you see.
Sort waste and recycle where possible.
Save water and power: switch off lights and air conditioning in empty rooms; fix leaks; run full loads in the laundry.
Explain these practices to guests and recommend licensed nature tours that protect wildlife.
Set a good example: guests copy what staff do.

head: Visitor action
Why
rows: Do not touch, stand on or take coral or shells
Coral is alive and breaks easily; taking it harms the reef.
Use reef-safe sunscreen
Some sunscreen ingredients harm coral.
Do not feed wild animals
It changes their behaviour and can make them aggressive or ill.
Stay on marked trails
It protects plants and keeps visitors safe.
Reuse towels
It saves water and power.
Take litter away or use the bins
Keeps beaches and rivers clean.

blocks.p: If a guest wants to break off a piece of coral to take home, **explain politely that the coral is alive and must stay**. Offer a better souvenir, such as a craft item from the local market.

blocks.note: Places such as Montego Bay and Negril have marine parks to protect the reefs. A villa on the coast can ask the guests to follow the park rules.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Professional standards and Team Jamaica at work

ul: A neat, clean, professional appearance gives visitors a **good first impression of Jamaica**.
Wear a clean uniform, keep your hair tidy, nails clean, and wear your name badge.
Be on time, ready for the day, and well rested.
Be honest, respectful, reliable and cheerful. Do not gossip about guests.

flow: Listen to the whole complaint without interrupting
Stay calm; do not argue or blame others
Apologise sincerely: 'I am sorry about that'
Say what you will do
Pass it to the person who can fix it, or fix it yourself if you can
Follow up and tell the guest the result
Record it

blocks.h: When a colleague is rude to a visitor

blocks.p: Help the visitor first, politely, and apologise. Then speak to your supervisor in private. Do not argue with your colleague in front of the guest.

blocks.h: Applying Team Jamaica every day at a villa or hotel

head: Job
How you apply Team Jamaica
rows: Gate and reception
Warm greeting, correct information, calm help if a vendor is bothering a guest.
Housekeeping
Respect privacy and property; knock and wait; report anything lost or damaged.
Kitchen and dining
Safe, clean food; honest answers about ingredients and allergens; friendly service.
Garden, pool and beach
Safety advice, watch children, keep walkways clear, report hazards.
Driving and transport
Licensed, safe, punctual, courteous.
All staff
Share Jamaica's story, protect the environment, treat everyone equally.

ul: Start the day neat and on time.
Greet every guest with a smile and use their name.
Answer questions honestly. Find out when you are not sure.
Recommend local food, attractions and licensed tours without pressure and without favouring those that pay you.
Give safety advice and know the emergency numbers.
Protect guests from harassment and report anyone who bothers them.
Look after the environment: save water and power; never litter.
Review your day: what went well, what could I do better?

blocks.note: Team Jamaica is not a set of rules for exams only. It is how a good Jamaican host behaves every day, with every guest, whether anyone is watching or not.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: I can say what Team Jamaica is, who runs it and who it is for.
I can explain why tourism workers are called ambassadors.
I can greet a visitor warmly and offer help.
I can speak clearly, with patience and honesty, to visitors who struggle with my accent.
I can say what visitor harassment is and give examples.
I can explain why harassment harms Jamaica.
I can prevent harassment and help a visitor who is being harassed, calmly and safely.
I can give safety advice on the sea, sun, valuables and transport.
I can name the emergency numbers: police 119, fire and ambulance 110.
I can help a guest who has lost a passport or had a bag stolen.
I can follow a hurricane plan and keep guests informed.
I can name Jamaica's national symbols and seven National Heroes.
I can give correct basic facts about history, parishes, music, food and places.
I can explain why coral must not be taken and what staff and visitors can do for the environment.
I can handle a complaint professionally and respond when a colleague is rude.
I can apply Team Jamaica in my own job.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each point and a practical example. For example: 'I accept a guest's no after offering a tour once, because pressure makes visitors feel unsafe and they may not return.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: A training programme for tourism workers, run by TPDCo.
The Tourism Product Development Company, which runs Team Jamaica.
Someone whose behaviour shows visitors what Jamaica is like.
Pressuring or bothering a visitor against their wishes.
A tour or transport provider approved to work with visitors.
A written record of what happened and what was done.
A villa's written plan for storm warnings.
Jamaica's Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management.
One of seven people honoured by the nation.
Africans who escaped slavery and lived free in the hills.
The first known people of Jamaica.
The Taíno name for the island, usually said to mean 'land of wood and water'.
The Jamaican language that mixes English with West African and other words.
1 August, the public holiday that marks the end of slavery.
6 August, when Jamaica became independent in 1962.
A living structure that protects the coast and shelters fish.
Sunscreen that does not harm coral.

c1.title: A vendor at the gate in Negril
c1.text: Trainee Shanice works at a beachfront villa in Negril. A British family has just arrived. A man outside the gate follows them up the path offering a boat tour, and when Mr Hughes says 'no, thank you' he steps in front of Mrs Hughes and keeps asking. The children look worried. Shanice is the only staff member at the gate.

c2.title: A lost wallet at a beach in Ocho Rios
c2.text: A guest, Mr Adeyemi from Nigeria, returns to the villa in Ocho Rios in a panic. He left his bag on the beach while he swam, and his wallet, bank cards and passport are gone. It is Saturday evening and his flight home is on Tuesday. Villa assistant Kayla is on duty.

c3.title: A hurricane warning in Port Antonio
c3.text: It is October. The Meteorological Service has issued a hurricane warning for the north-east coast. At a villa in Port Antonio, four guests are staying. The manager has a written hurricane plan. One guest wants to go on a day trip to the Blue Lagoon in the morning, and another is worried and asks what is going to happen.

c4.title: Questions about Jamaica at breakfast
c4.text: At a villa breakfast in Mandeville, a guest from Canada asks cook Tanisha what the black, green and gold flag means, which is the national bird, and who the Maroons were. Tanisha is not sure about one of the answers. The guest also asks if Tanisha can recommend a tour for the afternoon.

c5.title: Sun, sea and coral at a Treasure Beach villa
c5.text: A family staying at a villa in Treasure Beach spends a whole day at the beach. The father asks houseman Nathan if he can swim in the sea after dark with a few drinks in him, and the teenage daughter wants to take a piece of coral home. At 3 p.m. the mother feels faint after hours in the sun with no hat.

c6.title: A rude colleague at a Kingston guest house
c6.text: At a guest house in Kingston, a visitor from Germany complains to housekeeper Joy that the tour he booked was late and the driver was rude. Later that day, Joy hears another staff member speak sharply to the same visitor about his bill.

questions.q: What should Shanice do first when the man steps in front of Mrs Hughes?
o: Shout at him to go away and block the path with her arms
Move beside the family, say they are with her, and help them on
Tell the family to buy a tour so that he will leave them alone
Ignore him, because it is the guests' problem to settle on their own
questions.why: Stay calm and polite, step in safely and help the visitors move away. Shouting or blocking can lead to a fight, and ignoring the problem leaves the guests feeling unsafe.

questions.q: The man will not stop and keeps following the family. What should Shanice do next?
o: Walk the family to the house, and call 119 if he continues
Let the family decide whether to buy the tour from him
Follow the man down the road and insist that he leaves
Tell the family to leave the villa for the whole day
questions.why: If a person will not accept 'no' and continues to bother visitors, report it to security or the police on 119. Do not argue or confront the person alone.

questions.q: Later, a craft vendor shows Mr Hughes his carvings. Which behaviour by the vendor would be acceptable?
o: Showing his carvings once, and saying thank you when Mr Hughes declines
Putting a carving in Mrs Hughes's hand so that she feels she must buy it
Walking beside the family along the beach and lowering his price each time they say no
Asking the children to persuade their parents to buy
questions.why: Offering once and accepting the answer is courteous. Pushing an item into a visitor's hand, following them or pressuring them through their children is harassment, and it makes visitors feel unsafe.

questions.q: Mr Hughes later asks about a boat tour. How should Shanice recommend one?
o: Recommend the man at the gate, who has been very keen on it
Say that all boat tours are unsafe and should not be used
Suggest a licensed operator the villa knows, and explain it once
Book the first tour she can find and charge the villa account
questions.why: Recommend licensed, approved operators, explain the tour clearly once and let the guest decide. Do not favour someone because they pay or push hardest.

questions.q: What should Kayla do first for Mr Adeyemi?
o: Tell him to come back on Monday when the offices are open
Phone the police, then send him to look for the wallet by himself
Check he is calm and unhurt, then help him report it to the police
Tell him it is his own fault and that he should have used the safe
questions.why: First make sure the guest is safe and calm. Then help him report the loss to the police (119), because a police report is needed for his passport replacement and insurance.

questions.q: Besides the police, which body should Mr Adeyemi contact about his passport?
o: The local municipal corporation
His country's embassy or consulate
The villa's insurance company
The nearest airport desk
questions.why: A lost passport is dealt with by the guest's own embassy or consulate, which can issue a replacement or emergency travel document.

questions.q: What else should Kayla help Mr Adeyemi do at once?
o: Wait until Tuesday to cancel his cards at the airport
Call his bank to block the stolen cards
Buy him new cards from the villa's accounts
Ask the guests next door for money to lend him
questions.why: Stolen bank cards can be used within minutes, so the bank should be called at once to block them. Kayla should also write an incident report and tell her supervisor.

questions.q: A guest wants to go to the Blue Lagoon in the morning despite the warning. What should staff advise?
o: Go early, so that the trip is over before the storm arrives
Book a boat tour so that a guide can decide when it is safe
Stay at the villa and follow the plan and official advice
Go by taxi, because the road is quicker than going by boat
questions.why: In a hurricane warning guests should not travel to exposed places. Follow the villa's plan and instructions from the Meteorological Service and ODPEM.

questions.q: The worried guest asks what will happen. How should staff reply?
o: Explain calmly what the plan is, and keep them informed
Say that there is nothing to worry about, because storms often miss the island
Tell them to go to the airport at once and book any flight
Say that they will find out when the storm arrives
questions.why: Guests feel safer when staff are calm and clear. Explain the plan, say what you will do, and keep them informed. Do not make false promises.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in the villa's hurricane plan?
o: Opening every window so that the wind can blow right through
Securing loose items and shutters, and checking water and torches
Taking down the shutters so that the guests can watch the storm
Sending the staff home before the guests are settled in
questions.why: A hurricane plan covers securing the property, supplies such as water, torches and a first aid kit, and contact details for guests and emergency services.

questions.q: Tanisha is not sure which bird is the national bird. What should she do?
o: Say 'I will find out for you', check, and then tell the guest
Give her best guess so that the guest is not disappointed at all
Say that Jamaica has no national bird, as it has only symbols
Change the subject to the food and hope the guest forgets
questions.why: Honesty matters more than looking clever. A wrong answer spreads wrong facts; say you will find out, check a reliable source and report back. The national bird is the doctor bird.

questions.q: Which answer about the Maroons is correct?
o: Spanish settlers who ran the first sugar estates on the island
Taíno people who lived on the island before Columbus came
British soldiers who stayed on the island after 1655
Africans who escaped slavery and lived free in the hills
questions.why: Maroons were Africans who escaped from slavery and set up free communities in the hills. Accompong and Moore Town are Maroon towns today.

questions.q: The guest asks Tanisha to recommend an afternoon tour. What is the best way to answer?
o: Recommend only the tour from which she gets a commission
Say that she cannot give any advice at all about tours
Describe one tour and tell the guest it is the only safe one
Suggest two licensed tours that suit the guest, and explain them
questions.why: Give honest advice about licensed operators that suit the guest, explain once, and let the guest choose. Do not push or favour a tour for personal gain.

questions.q: The father asks about swimming in the sea after dark after drinking. What should Nathan advise?
o: It is fine, if he swims close to the shore and does not go far
He should not; swimming at night or after alcohol is unsafe
He may go if his daughter swims with him all the time
He may go if he stays in the shallow water by the beach
questions.why: Swimming in the dark or after drinking alcohol is dangerous because help is hard to see and judgement is poor. Advise swimming only in daylight, where it is safe.

questions.q: The daughter wants to take a piece of coral home. What is the best reply?
o: Let her take it, as there is plenty of coral on the beach
Explain that coral is alive and must stay; suggest a craft souvenir
Tell her it is against the law and she will be arrested at once
Tell her that coral is dangerous to touch and to leave it alone
questions.why: Coral is a living animal that protects the coast and shelters fish. Explain politely why it must stay, and suggest a local craft item as a souvenir.

questions.q: The mother feels faint after hours in the sun. What should Nathan do?
o: Move her to shade, give water and get help if she is no better
Tell her to lie in the sun until the faint feeling passes
Give her a hot drink and carry on with the rest of the day
Send her back to the beach to cool off in the sea for a while
questions.why: Move a faint person to the shade, give water, loosen tight clothing and watch her. Call 110 if she does not recover quickly.

questions.q: What is the best way for Joy to handle the German visitor's complaint about the tour?
o: Tell him that the tour company is always late and nothing can be done
Listen, apologise, and pass it to someone who can fix it
Explain that it was his fault for booking a cheap tour
Tell him to speak to the driver himself
questions.why: Listen without interrupting, apologise sincerely and pass the problem to the person who can resolve it. Tell the guest who will help.

questions.q: Joy hears a colleague speak sharply to the visitor. What should she do?
o: Tell the visitor that the colleague has had a very bad day
Argue with the colleague in front of the guest
Say nothing, because it is not her job to speak up
Help the visitor politely, then see the supervisor in private
questions.why: The visitor comes first: help him and apologise. Then report the matter to the supervisor in private, so that the guest does not see staff arguing.

questions.q: On which day each year is National Heroes' Day observed in Jamaica?
o: The third Monday in October
The first Monday in August
The last Friday in November
The second Monday in January
questions.why: National Heroes' Day is held on the third Monday in October, to honour Jamaica's seven National Heroes.

questions.q: Which event did National Hero Sam Sharpe lead in 1831?
o: The Morant Bay Rebellion
The Christmas Rebellion (the Baptist War)
The founding of the Maroon town of Accompong
The march for Jamaica's independence
questions.why: Sam Sharpe led the 1831 Christmas Rebellion, also called the Baptist War, which helped bring slavery to an end. The Morant Bay Rebellion was led by Paul Bogle in 1865.
